claims.feature: incidental figure given a full death
claims.claim: Rettino cites the Kanlin messenger killed with Spring Rain's letter, an 'incidental figure' living the drama of his own life and death, as Kay's device for showing history's lost documents.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: living through the drama and passion of his own life

claims.claim: Rettino argues Kay's endings grant refuge to a few characters rather than reversing historical catastrophe: a happy ending weighted with sorrow.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: a happy ending, though one weighted with sorrow

claims.claim: Rettino notes Jehane sees 'a good man raise his sword and... a good man fall' with deliberate ambiguity, resolved only in the epilogue.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: With deliberate ambiguity on Kay’s part

claims.claim: Rettino reads Tai's recognition scene as a false assumption about his role in shaping history, with Sima Zian calling such knowledge arrogance.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: a false assumption about his role in shaping history

claims.claim: Rettino cites the narrator's essayistic passage that humans demand order and pattern in the flux of history, exposing Kay's own patterning.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: questions the integrity of historical narratives

claims.claim: Rettino notes Under Heaven closes on two unnamed men burying the dead until they die and the spirits fall silent.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: not even the dead can grieve forever

claims.claim: Rettino reads Ammar's closing poem as setting an elegiac tone, with children's laughter audible through the window.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: The poem sets an elegiac tone

claims.claim: Rettino reads Baerd carrying memory 'like a cart yoked to his shoulders' and Alessan's blade-in-the-soul oath as memory chosen as bondage rather than escape.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: like a cart yoked to his shoulders

claims.claim: Rettino terms Kay's settings 'mirror worlds' that distort a historical original so its story can be projected onto other contexts.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: The Palm is a “mirror world” of Italy

claims.claim: Rettino, via Mendlesohn, finds it troubling that Tigana relies on the incontestable club-story authority of guides (Baerd, Alessan) in a novel about how power controls history.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: it is somewhat troubling that Kay should choose

claims.claim: Cobb argues Kay's enrichment of the reader is primarily emotional rather than rational, helping readers bear the burden of history rather than master it.
claims.source: Christopher Cobb, 'Guy Gavriel Kay and the Psychology of History', Foundation (Summer 2005), reprinted on Bright Weavings

claims.claim: Cobb reads the Tigana oath as memory that is both a wound and a rod of support.
claims.source: Christopher Cobb, 'Guy Gavriel Kay and the Psychology of History', Foundation (Summer 2005), reprinted on Bright Weavings
claims.quote: This memory is both a wound and a rod of support

claims.claim: Cobb notes it is perfectly possible to read Tigana without knowing it recasts Renaissance Italy, so its revision uncomfortably resembles the tyrant's spell.
claims.source: Christopher Cobb, 'Guy Gavriel Kay and the Psychology of History', Foundation (Summer 2005), reprinted on Bright Weavings
claims.quote: perfectly possible to read the novel without any awareness

claims.claim: Cobb observes that the Sarantine Mosaic's minimal adaptation of place-names and extensive acknowledgements force the reader to recognise actual history.
claims.source: Christopher Cobb, 'Guy Gavriel Kay and the Psychology of History', Foundation (Summer 2005), reprinted on Bright Weavings

claims.claim: Cobb reads Crispin's mosaic as an analogy for Kay's own project of re-creating history in art.
claims.source: Christopher Cobb, 'Guy Gavriel Kay and the Psychology of History', Foundation (Summer 2005), reprinted on Bright Weavings
claims.quote: makes an analogy between his own artistic project and Crispin’s
